subject: literature
title: Shanghai Modernism and Eileen Chang, c. 1928–1952: dance halls, war and a woman writer's city
dek: Between the late 1920s and the Communist victory, Shanghai was China's biggest, richest and most foreign-shaped city, and it produced a literature to match. This lesson moves from the New Sensationists, who wrote about nightclubs and speeding cars, through the left-wing writers who wanted literature to serve revolution, to Eileen Chang (張愛玲), who became the most famous young writer in Japanese-occupied Shanghai and later shaped generations of women writers in Taiwan.
era: c. 1928–1952, from the first Shanghai modernist magazines to Eileen Chang's departure for Hong Kong, with an afterlife in Taiwan and Hong Kong from the 1960s
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in the English Wikipedia articles on Eileen Chang, the New Sensationists, Liu Na'ou, Mu Shiying, Shi Zhecun, Dai Wangshu, the League of Left-Wing Writers, Su Qing, Ding Ling and Xiao Hong, and on the novellas and films named here. Dates of birth, death and publication follow those articles. Where sources differ on small details, such as exact magazine issues, the lesson leaves the detail out rather than guess. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Shanghai massacre
timeline.detail: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists turn on their Communist allies in Shanghai in April. The city becomes the Nationalist government's financial centre, while left-wing writers work under the threat of arrest.

timeline.label: Dai Wangshu's first book
timeline.detail: Dai Wangshu publishes the poetry collection My Memory (我的記憶). His French-influenced lyric poems become the poetry side of Shanghai modernism.

timeline.label: Urban Scenes and the Left League
timeline.detail: Liu Na'ou, a Taiwanese writer living in Shanghai, publishes the story collection Urban Scenes (都市風景線). On 2 March the League of Left-Wing Writers is founded in Shanghai, with Lu Xun giving the opening address.

timeline.label: Five Martyrs
timeline.detail: On 7 February the Nationalist authorities execute five League members, including Rou Shi and Hu Yepin. Literature in Shanghai is now openly political and dangerous.

timeline.label: Les Contemporains
timeline.detail: Shi Zhecun edits the monthly Les Contemporains (現代), which publishes Mu Shiying, Dai Wangshu and large numbers of translations of foreign literature.

timeline.label: War and the 'Orphan Island'
timeline.detail: Japan attacks Shanghai. The Chinese parts of the city fall, but the International Settlement and French Concession remain foreign-run islands surrounded by occupied territory until December 1941.

timeline.label: Two assassinations
timeline.detail: Mu Shiying (28 June) and Liu Na'ou (3 September) are shot dead in Shanghai while working for newspapers under Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government.

timeline.label: Hong Kong falls
timeline.detail: Japan takes Hong Kong in December. Eileen Chang, one semester short of her degree at the University of Hong Kong, returns to Shanghai the next year.

timeline.label: Chang's breakout year
timeline.detail: With the help of the editor Zhou Shoujuan, Chang publishes a run of stories including Love in a Fallen City (傾城之戀) and The Golden Cangue (金鎖記). She meets Hu Lancheng.

timeline.label: Romances
timeline.detail: Chang's story collection Romances (傳奇) sells out quickly. Su Qing's autobiographical novel Ten Years of Marriage (結婚十年) is another wartime bestseller. Chang and Hu Lancheng marry privately.

timeline.label: Written on Water and Japan's surrender
timeline.detail: Chang publishes her essay collection Written on Water (流言). After Japan surrenders, writers who published under the occupation face suspicion.

timeline.label: New China and departure
timeline.detail: The Communists take Shanghai in May 1949. Chang leaves for Hong Kong in 1952 and moves to the United States in 1955.

timeline.label: C. T. Hsia's history
timeline.detail: C. T. Hsia's A History of Modern Chinese Fiction gives Chang a major place in the canon. Her rediscovery in Taiwan and Hong Kong begins in the 1960s.

timeline.label: Death in Los Angeles
timeline.detail: Chang is found dead in her Westwood apartment on 8 September. Her ashes are scattered in the Pacific.

timeline.label: Lust, Caution on screen
timeline.detail: Ang Lee's film of Chang's novella Lust, Caution wins the Golden Lion at Venice.

fun_fact.title: 'Be famous early'
fun_fact.text: Eileen Chang is still quoted all over the Chinese-speaking world for one line from the preface to the second edition of Romances in 1944: 出名要趁早呀！ — roughly, 'You have to become famous early!' She went on to say that if it comes too late, the happiness is not as sharp. The English Wikipedia article gives it as: 'To be famous, I must hurry. If it comes too late, it will not bring me so much happiness ... Hurry, hurry, or it will be too late, too late!' She was 23 or 24 when she wrote it, and she was right about the timing: her years of greatest fame in Shanghai lasted only from 1943 to 1945.

sections.title: A treaty port that became China's modern city

blocks.text: Shanghai's modern history begins with defeat. After the First Opium War, the 1842 Treaty of Nanking opened Shanghai to British trade, and foreign powers soon carved out their own districts. By the 1920s the city had two foreign-run zones, the International Settlement (dominated by Britain and later also Japan and the United States) and the French Concession, wrapped around Chinese-governed districts. Chinese law did not fully apply inside the foreign zones. That made them a refuge for exiles, radicals, publishers and gangsters alike.

By the early 1930s Shanghai was China's largest city and its centre of banking, shipping, film, advertising and publishing. It had department stores, neon signs, jazz bands, dance halls, cinemas showing Hollywood films, and the country's biggest printing houses. Most of China was rural and poor; Shanghai was the place where Chinese readers first met the modern city at full speed.

Literature arrived there already divided. The May Fourth movement of 1919 had demanded a new literature in plain vernacular Chinese that would criticise tradition and wake the nation up. At the same time, Shanghai's mass market loved what critics dismissively called the Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies school: serialised romances and melodramas in newspapers and magazines. Zhang Henshui's Fate in Tears and Laughter (啼笑因緣, 1930) was one huge hit of this kind. Serious writers looked down on such fiction, but the young Eileen Chang read it with pleasure, and she would later combine popular melodrama with modernist psychology.

sections.title: The New Sensationists: writing at the speed of the city

blocks.text: In the late 1920s a small circle of young writers, several of whom had studied French at the Jesuit-run Aurora University, began writing fiction about the city itself. They became known as the New Sensationists (新感覺派). The name came from Japan, where writers such as Yokomitsu Riichi and Kawabata Yasunari had launched the Shinkankakuha, or New Sensation school, in the mid-1920s, borrowing techniques from European modernism. The Shanghai group was more interested in the unconscious, in sensation and in style than in social reform.

The surprising founder figure is Liu Na'ou (劉吶鷗, 1905–1940). He was born Liu Tsan-po in Liouying, Tainan, in Japanese-ruled Taiwan, studied in Tokyo, and moved to Shanghai in 1926. Because he read Japanese, he could bring Shinkankakuha methods straight into Chinese. His collection Urban Scenes (都市風景線, 1930) shows men and women chasing each other through racecourses, cafés and dance floors, with sentences cut up like film montage. Liu also produced films and wrote about cinema, and his 1927 diary is now held by the National Museum of Taiwan Literature in Tainan.

Mu Shiying (穆時英, 1912–1940) became the group's most dazzling stylist. A banker's son and, by reputation, an excellent dancer, he set his stories in cabarets and nightclubs. 'Shanghai Fox-trot' (上海的狐步舞) and 'Five in a Nightclub' (夜總會裡的五個人) repeat phrases like music, jump between viewpoints and describe the city as a machine of desire and exhaustion. Shi Zhecun (施蟄存, 1905–2003) wrote quieter psychological stories, such as 'One Evening in the Rainy Season' (梅雨之夕), in which a married man's fantasy about a stranger under his umbrella fills a short walk home. The poet Dai Wangshu (戴望舒, 1905–1950), whose 'Rain Alley' (雨巷) is still taught in schools, brought French symbolist music into Chinese verse.

Their main platform was Les Contemporains (現代), the monthly magazine Shi Zhecun edited from 1932 to 1935. It published new Chinese writing alongside a large amount of translated foreign literature, much of it American and Japanese, and introduced readers to modern art movements. If you have read the High Modernism lesson, you can think of Les Contemporains as Shanghai's version of the little magazines of London and Paris.

sections.title: The Left League: literature as a weapon

blocks.text: Not everyone thought writing about dance halls was a good use of talent while the country faced civil war, poverty and Japanese pressure. On 2 March 1930, writers close to the Chinese Communist Party founded the League of Left-Wing Writers in Shanghai. Lu Xun (魯迅), the most respected writer of the May Fourth generation and not himself a Party member, gave the opening address. The League grew from about fifty members to several hundred and asked writers to destroy the old society's ways of thought and serve political movements.

The Nationalist government banned the League within months. On 7 February 1931 it executed five League members, among them the writers Rou Shi (柔石) and Hu Yepin (胡也頻), after a mass arrest. They became known as the Five Martyrs of the Left League. Hu Yepin's partner was Ding Ling (丁玲, 1904–1986), whose 1928 story 'Miss Sophie's Diary' (莎菲女士的日記) had shocked readers with a young woman's frank account of her own desire and boredom. After 1931 Ding Ling moved firmly to the left, was imprisoned by the Nationalists, and later went to the Communist base at Yan'an.

The big realist novels of the decade also came out of Shanghai's publishing world: Mao Dun's Midnight (子夜, 1933), about speculators and factory owners in Shanghai itself; Ba Jin's Family (家), serialised from 1931, about young people breaking out of a patriarchal household; and Cao Yu's play Thunderstorm (雷雨, 1934). In 1932 a public debate broke out over whether a writer could be on the left and still remain independent, the so-called 'third category' argument. Dai Wangshu defended that independence against Lu Xun's harder line. The quarrel between art for its own sake and art for the revolution would shape Chinese literature for decades, and it returns in the Misty Poetry lesson.

Women writers worked across these camps. Xiao Hong (蕭紅, 1911–1942) arrived in Shanghai from the northeast in 1934, and Lu Xun helped publish her novel The Field of Life and Death (生死場, 1935), about peasant life and the bodies of rural women under famine and Japanese occupation. She later wrote Tales of Hulan River (呼蘭河傳) and died in Japanese-occupied Hong Kong in January 1942, aged thirty.

In 1937 Japan attacked Shanghai. After months of fighting, the Chinese districts fell, but the International Settlement and the French Concession stayed under foreign control, surrounded by Japanese-held territory. This four-year period is called the Orphan Island (孤島). Publishing went on inside the island, often in coded or escapist forms. Many writers left for the interior; Shi Zhecun, for example, went to Yunnan and turned to classical scholarship.

In 1940 Japan set up a collaborationist Chinese government under Wang Jingwei (汪精衛) in Nanjing. Both Mu Shiying and Liu Na'ou took jobs running newspapers under that regime, and both were shot dead in Shanghai that year, Mu on 28 June and Liu on 3 September, by assassins generally attributed to Nationalist underground forces. The two men who had written the most glamorous pages of Shanghai modernism died in its most violent streets.

In December 1941, after Pearl Harbor, Japanese troops entered the foreign settlements too. From then until August 1945 all of Shanghai was occupied. Anti-Japanese writing was impossible and openly pro-Japanese writing was shameful, so the literature that thrived was about private life: marriage, money, families and love. That was exactly the space in which two young women, Eileen Chang and Su Qing, became the city's best-selling writers.

sections.title: Eileen Chang: the aristocrat's granddaughter who wrote about everyday ruin

blocks.text: Eileen Chang was born Zhang Ying (張煐) in Shanghai on 30 September 1920. Her family was old Qing nobility in decline: her paternal grandmother was a daughter of the statesman Li Hongzhang. Her father was addicted to opium and kept concubines; her mother, Huang Suqiong, left to study in Europe and later divorced him. When Chang was about ten, her mother renamed her Ailing, a transliteration of the English name Eileen, so she could enter an English-language school. At eighteen, after a quarrel, her father beat her and locked her in a room for months while she was ill with dysentery; she escaped to live with her mother. This family of faded grandeur, opium, quarrels over money and trapped women became the raw material of her fiction.

Chang won a place at the University of London in 1939 but could not go because of the war, so she studied English literature at the University of Hong Kong instead. When Japan took Hong Kong in December 1941, she was one semester short of her degree. She went back to Shanghai in 1942 and began writing for magazines. In 1943 the veteran editor Zhou Shoujuan, a leading figure of the popular Mandarin Ducks and Butterflies world, published her stories, and within two years she was the most talked-about new writer in the city.

Two novellas from 1943 show what she could do. Love in a Fallen City (傾城之戀) follows Bai Liusu, a divorced woman humiliated by her family in Shanghai, who goes to Hong Kong to win the playboy Fan Liuyuan. Their careful game of courtship is only settled when the Japanese attack destroys the colony; the fall of a whole city, the narrator suggests, may have happened so that one woman could get married. The Golden Cangue (金鎖記) is darker. Cao Qiqiao, a sesame-oil shopkeeper's daughter, is married into a rich family to an invalid husband. She spends decades guarding the money she finally inherits, and in the process ruins the lives of her own son and daughter. The cangue of the title is a wooden collar once used to punish prisoners; hers is made of gold. The translator and critic Fu Lei praised the story highly, and C. T. Hsia later called it the greatest novelette in the history of Chinese literature.

Chang's style mixed things that critics usually kept apart. Her plots are the stuff of popular melodrama: arranged marriages, mistresses, inheritances. Her sentences borrow the rhythms of the classic novel Dream of the Red Chamber, which she loved. But her attention to clothes, furniture, light, smell and the small cruelties people inflict on each other is fully modern, and she refuses to give readers heroes or political lessons. Other well-known stories from these years include 'Sealed Off' (封鎖), set in a tram stopped during an air-raid blockade, and 'Red Rose, White Rose' (紅玫瑰與白玫瑰). Her stories were collected in Romances (傳奇, 1944), which became a bestseller, and her essays in Written on Water (流言, 1945).

Her private life became part of her legend. In 1943 she met Hu Lancheng (胡蘭成), a writer and official in the Wang Jingwei government, who was still married at the time. They married privately in 1944. Hu soon began other relationships, fled under a false identity after Japan's defeat, and the couple divorced in 1947. After the war, Chang's association with Hu and with occupation-era magazines damaged her reputation. Hu later lived in Japan and lectured in Taiwan in the 1970s, where he influenced the Chu sisters, a link you can follow in the Taiwan Women's Fiction lesson.

sections.title: Su Qing and the other women of occupied Shanghai

blocks.text: Chang was not alone. Su Qing (蘇青, 1914–1982), born in Ningbo, had left university to marry a husband chosen by her family. After an unhappy marriage of about ten years, she divorced and began supporting herself as a writer and editor. Her autobiographical novel Ten Years of Marriage (結婚十年, 1944) described marriage, childbirth and divorce from a wife's point of view with a bluntness readers had rarely seen, and it sold extremely well. She also ran her own magazine. Chang and Su Qing knew each other and were often compared, sometimes as rivals and sometimes as the two voices of women's wartime Shanghai.

Their success has always raised hard questions. Both published under Japanese occupation, in an environment where politics had been pushed out of print. Some critics have seen their focus on domestic life as an evasion. Others argue that writing honestly about women's economic dependence, loveless marriages and divorce was its own kind of seriousness at a time when nationalist literature usually treated women as symbols of the suffering nation. After 1949 Su Qing stayed on the mainland, was attacked for her wartime associations, was imprisoned in 1955, and died poor in 1982.

sections.title: What else was happening in city literature at the same time

blocks.text: Shanghai's modernism was part of a worldwide moment when writers tried to capture the big city. In Berlin, Alfred Döblin's Berlin Alexanderplatz (1929) used montage, advertising slogans and overheard speech to show a working-class man lost in the metropolis, much as Mu Shiying did with Shanghai. Irmgard Keun's The Artificial Silk Girl (1932) followed a young woman trying to make her way in Weimar Berlin, a cousin to Chang's and Su Qing's heroines. In Tokyo, the Shinkankakuha writers who inspired Liu Na'ou were doing the same for their own fast-changing capital.

In New York, the Harlem Renaissance was winding down by the mid-1930s; in Paris, Black students were launching Négritude; both lessons show other cities where a colonised or marginalised people built a modern literature in a metropolis that was not entirely theirs. Closer to home, Taiwan under Japanese rule had its own modernists. In 1933 Yang Chi-chang (楊熾昌) and friends in Tainan founded the Le Moulin poetry society (風車詩社), writing surrealist poetry in Japanese, while Yang Kui's story 'The Newspaper Boy' (送報伕) won recognition in a Tokyo magazine in 1934. Liu Na'ou, a Tainan native in Shanghai, is a living link between these worlds.

Shanghai's film industry ran in parallel. The actress Ruan Lingyu (阮玲玉) starred in New Women (新女性, 1935), about a woman writer destroyed by gossip and the press, and killed herself on 8 March 1935, leaving a note blaming malicious gossip. Her story shows how the same modern city that offered women new careers also exposed them to a cruel new mass media, a theme that runs through Chang's fiction as well.

sections.title: Silence in Shanghai, fever in Taiwan

blocks.text: When the Communists took Shanghai in 1949, the city's modernist and popular traditions were both judged bourgeois. Shi Zhecun turned to classical scholarship and was labelled a rightist in 1957. Chang tried for a while to adapt, publishing the novel Eighteen Springs (十八春) under the pen name Liang Jing, which she later rewrote as Half a Lifelong Romance (半生緣). In 1952 she left for Hong Kong, where she worked for the United States Information Service and wrote two anti-Communist novels in English, The Rice-Sprout Song and Naked Earth. In 1955 she moved to the United States, married the American screenwriter Ferdinand Reyher in 1956, and struggled for years to succeed as an English-language novelist.

Her second life began in criticism. C. T. Hsia's A History of Modern Chinese Fiction (1961) put Chang alongside Lu Xun as a major writer. Taiwan's Crown publishing house reissued her work, and from the late 1960s an 'Eileen Chang fever' took hold in Taiwan and Hong Kong. Writers such as Chu T'ien-wen and Chu T'ien-hsin were so clearly influenced that critics spoke of a Chang school (張派). In Taiwan in the late 1970s she published Lust, Caution (色，戒), a short spy story about a young woman sent to seduce and trap a collaborator, which she had worked on for more than twenty years. She also translated the nineteenth-century Shanghai courtesan novel The Sing-song Girls of Shanghai (海上花列傳) from Wu dialect into Mandarin and English; Hou Hsiao-hsien later filmed it as Flowers of Shanghai.

Chang lived increasingly alone in Los Angeles and was found dead in her Westwood apartment on 8 September 1995, several days after she had died. Since then her reputation has only grown. Unpublished works have appeared, including Little Reunions (小團圓, 2009), a thinly veiled account of her life with Hu Lancheng, and Ang Lee's film of Lust, Caution won the Golden Lion in Venice in 2007. On the mainland, where she had been ignored for decades, Wang Anyi's novel The Song of Everlasting Sorrow (長恨歌, 1995) revived the image of old Shanghai through the life of one woman, and readers immediately compared it to Chang. In 1999 the scholar Leo Ou-fan Lee's book Shanghai Modern brought Liu Na'ou, Mu Shiying, Shi Zhecun and Chang back together as one story of Chinese urban modernity.

sections.title: Why this matters for reading women's writing

items: Shanghai modernism shows that Chinese modern literature was not only about national crisis. It was also about consumer goods, cinema, sex, money and loneliness in a big city.
The New Sensationists tied China to Tokyo and Paris; one of their founders was Taiwanese, which makes this part of Taiwan's literary history too.
Eileen Chang and Su Qing made women's domestic and economic lives the centre of serious fiction, at a time when politics usually treated women as symbols rather than people.
Their careers also show how wartime politics, collaboration and personal relationships can shape a woman writer's reputation for decades, often more harshly than a man's.
Chang's later fame in Taiwan explains a lot about the Taiwanese women's fiction of the 1970s to 1990s that you met in an earlier lesson.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Eileen Chang wrote her best-known stories under a foreign occupation and refused to write political fiction. Is choosing to write about marriage, money and family during a war a retreat from history, or a different way of recording it? As you think about which organisations and stories cool dairy might highlight, consider whose everyday lives tend to be left out of 'big' history, and how a writer like Chang or Su Qing changes that.
